paragraphs.text: A loose [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan. Raw is the undarkened branch of pu’er, the one never given shou’s fast fermentation. Its leaf comes from the province’s large leaf tea trees. It is withered, then fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making), rolled, and dried in the sun. The heat stops most of the leaf’s own enzymes but not all. Because the leaf is never hot air dried afterwards, the activity that survives is what lets the tea keep changing for years. This one was never pressed. It is sold loose, as the rough tea called [maocha](sheng:processing).

Without a fermenting pile, raw pu’er [changes gradually in storage](sheng:aging), so the conditions it has been kept in become part of its history. Heat and humidity set the pace, because the change comes partly from slow oxidation and partly from microbes. [Warm, humid stores](sheng:storage) move it quickly. Cool, dry ones move it slowly, and a store that is too dry can leave it stalled and green.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.
